message.content:
You are a Whoosh expert. From knowledge of Whoosh's PUBLIC documented behavior (no source access):

1. What is the default analyzer for a whoosh.fields.TEXT field? Name its exact component chain.
2. What is the default regular expression used by Whoosh's RegexTokenizer / StandardAnalyzer default? Write it out.
3. What is Whoosh's default English stop word list (whoosh.analysis.STOP_WORDS)? List every word you believe is in it.
4. What is the default minsize for StopFilter in StandardAnalyzer, and what does minsize do?
5. What is the default analyzer for a whoosh.fields.ID field, and how does it tokenize "the quick brown fox"?
6. TEXT(stored=True) vs TEXT(): what does stored change?

Then: this is being ported to JavaScript. Python's re \w on a str is unicode-aware; JavaScript's \w is ASCII-only. Specify the exact JS regex (with flags) that best reproduces Python's \w for tokenization, and explain the failure mode if bare \w were used with input like "héllo 世界".

content.text: Whoosh is not installed here, so items 1–6 are recall. I did empirically verify the Python-vs-JS regex semantics (stdlib `re` and Node), which is the part that must be exactly right.

input.lens: Whoosh analyzer-chain recall, calibrated by confidence, then Python→JS Unicode/regex fidelity for the port. Items 1-6 are from memory of Whoosh's public docs/API (no Whoosh installed in /workspace — confirmed `ModuleNotFoundError`), so each carries an explicit confidence and a one-line verification command. Item 7 is not recall: I empirically tested Python 3 `re` and Node against the same inputs, so its claims are measured, not remembered.

conclusions.answer: StandardAnalyzer(). Exact chain, in order: RegexTokenizer(expression=default_pattern, gaps=False) | LowercaseFilter() | StopFilter(stoplist=STOP_WORDS, minsize=2, maxsize=None). StandardAnalyzer is a composition function, not a class — it returns a CompositeAnalyzer of those three links. The StopFilter link is conditional: StandardAnalyzer(stoplist=None) returns only RegexTokenizer | LowercaseFilter. Note there is NO stemming — that is StemmingAnalyzer (RegexTokenizer | LowercaseFilter | StopFilter | StemFilter), which TEXT does not use by default.
conclusions.confidence: High — this is the canonical documented chain and the three-link shape is stable across Whoosh 2.x.
conclusions.implementation_note: Port as three composable stages over a token stream, not one regex pass. Also mirror TEXT's other defaults: phrase=True (positions recorded, so your token objects need pos) and no field_boost change. Keep the stages separately swappable — the stoplist=None case must drop the third stage entirely rather than pass an empty set, because an empty stoplist still applies minsize.

conclusions.answer: r"\w+(\.?\w+)*" — exposed publicly as whoosh.analysis.tokenizers.default_pattern (a precompiled pattern). Semantics: one or more word chars, then zero or more repetitions of (optional single dot + one or more word chars). Consequences: "www.example.com" and "1.5" survive as single tokens; a sentence-final dot in "end." is NOT consumed (the tail requires word chars after the dot), so you get "end"; "a..b" yields "a" and "b" (only a single dot may bridge). gaps=False by default means the regex matches the tokens themselves, not the separators — gaps=True inverts it to re.split behavior.
conclusions.confidence: High on the pattern text; high on the dot-bridging behavior (verified by running that exact pattern under Python 3 re in this session).
conclusions.implementation_note: Do not 'simplify' this to \w+ during the port. The dot-bridging is load-bearing for URLs, decimals, and version strings, and dropping it silently changes which documents match. Convert the capturing group to non-capturing in JS: (?:\.?...)* — the group is never read, and leaving it capturing costs you on every match.

conclusions.answer: A frozenset of ~34 short words. My belief, complete list: a, an, and, are, as, at, be, by, can, for, from, have, if, in, is, it, may, not, of, on, or, tbd, that, the, this, to, us, we, when, will, with, yet, you, your. Two things I am confident about structurally even if a word or two is off: (a) it is deliberately TINY — ~34 entries vs ~179 in NLTK's English list — so it is NOT a general-purpose English stoplist; (b) it contains the distinctly non-English-prose entry 'tbd', a fingerprint of Whoosh's origins as a documentation/help indexer. Notably ABSENT (do not add them): was, were, been, but, they, he, she, his, her, all, would, there, what, which, who, how, do, no, so, than, then, these. StopFilter also accepts lang=, which pulls a much larger per-language list from whoosh.lang.stopwords instead.
conclusions.confidence: MEDIUM — this is the weakest item in this report and the one most likely to be off by a word or two. Treat the list as a hypothesis, not a spec.
conclusions.implementation_note: Verify before porting, do not trust me: `python -c "from whoosh.analysis import STOP_WORDS; print(len(STOP_WORDS)); print(sorted(STOP_WORDS))"` and paste the literal output into the JS source as a frozen Set. A wrong stoplist is the worst class of porting bug here because it fails silently — no error, just different recall on a subset of queries, and it corrupts index and query symmetrically so round-trip tests still pass. Any 1-character entry you think you see is redundant anyway (minsize=2 already removes it).

conclusions.topic: 4. StopFilter minsize in StandardAnalyzer, and what minsize does
conclusions.answer: minsize=2 (and maxsize=None, i.e. no upper bound). minsize removes any token whose text length is strictly less than minsize, so the default drops all 1-character tokens. It is a pure character-length test applied after LowercaseFilter, entirely independent of the stoplist — a token is dropped if it is in the stoplist OR shorter than minsize OR (if maxsize set) longer than maxsize. Practical consequence people trip on: single letters and single digits are unsearchable in a default TEXT field — "Vitamin C", "Plan B", "Section 5", "C" all lose that token. StopFilter also defaults to renumber=True, which closes the positional gaps left by removed tokens, so phrase queries spanning a removed stopword behave as if the stopword were never there.
conclusions.confidence: High on minsize=2 and maxsize=None; high on the strictly-less-than boundary (2-char tokens are kept); slightly lower on renumber=True being the default, though I believe it is.
conclusions.implementation_note: Subtle JS trap: Python len() counts code points, JS .length counts UTF-16 code units. An astral-plane single character (e.g. U+1D400, or many CJK extension chars) is len 1 in Python — dropped — but .length 2 in JS — kept. Use [...token].length (or a code-point counter) for the minsize/maxsize comparison, never .length. Conversely, decomposed 'é' is len 2 in Python, so NFD text can slip past minsize in Python where NFC text would not — another reason to fix normalization explicitly (see item 7).

conclusions.topic: 5. Default analyzer for whoosh.fields.ID, and "the quick brown fox"
conclusions.answer: IDAnalyzer(), which is just a bare IDTokenizer() (it appends a LowercaseFilter only if you pass lowercase=True). IDTokenizer emits the entire field value as exactly ONE token, verbatim. So "the quick brown fox" tokenizes to a single token: "the quick brown fox" — spaces preserved, case preserved, no stopword removal, no minsize filtering, position 0. It is therefore findable only by the exact whole-string term, e.g. ID:"the quick brown fox"; searching ID:quick matches nothing. (IDAnalyzer is documented as deprecated in favor of using IDTokenizer directly, but ID still defaults to it.) Empty string yields zero tokens.
conclusions.confidence: High — this whole-value-as-one-term behavior is the entire point of the ID field type.
conclusions.implementation_note: In JS this is a one-line stage: yield a single token with text = the raw value, pos 0, startChar 0, endChar = value.length. Do not route ID values through your text pipeline's trim/lowercase helpers — the case and internal whitespace sensitivity is intentional and is what makes ID usable as a primary key with unique=True. If your port needs case-insensitive IDs, that must be an explicit IDAnalyzer(lowercase=True) equivalent, mirrored on the query side.

conclusions.answer: stored only controls retrievability, never searchability. With stored=True, Whoosh saves the ORIGINAL pre-analysis value in the document's stored-fields record, so it comes back in results (hit["body"], hit.fields(), searcher.stored_fields(docnum)). With the default stored=False, the field is still fully indexed, searched, and scored identically — you just get a KeyError / missing key when you try to read it off a Hit, because the value was never kept. What stored does NOT change: the analyzer chain, the terms written to the index, scoring, or matching. What it costs: index size (a full copy of the text). What it enables: displaying the text, and highlighting — whoosh.highlight needs the original text, which it normally takes from the stored field (otherwise you must pass the text in yourself, or add term vectors).
conclusions.implementation_note: Keep the stored copy in a separate per-document blob keyed by docnum, distinct from the inverted index, so the two concerns stay independently optimizable. Preserve the important detail that the stored value is the raw input, NOT the analyzed/lowercased/stopped tokens — reconstructing display text from the token stream is lossy and is a classic port regression. Whoosh also supports overriding the stored value via a _stored_<fieldname> key in add_document; decide up front whether your port needs that escape hatch.

conclusions.topic: 7. Exact JS regex reproducing Python's \w for tokenization, + bare-\w failure mode
conclusions.answer:
USE: /[\p{L}\p{N}_]+(?:\.?[\p{L}\p{N}_]+)*/gu

Flags: g (iterate all matches via matchAll/exec, matching re.finditer) and u (REQUIRED — it is what enables \p{...} and switches to code-point semantics so astral-plane letters match as one character). Do NOT add i: the tokenizer is case-sensitive and lowercasing is a separate downstream filter. Add d only if you want explicit indices; matchAll already gives m.index, and endChar = m.index + m[0].length. The ES2024 v flag works in place of u if you prefer set notation.

WHY that character class is exact: Python documents str-mode \w as 'alphanumeric characters (as defined by str.isalnum()) as well as the underscore'. I measured the actual category coverage: é(Ll) 世(Lo) ʰ(Lm) ٣(Nd) ½(No) Ⅷ(Nl) all match; U+0301 combining acute (Mn), U+203F undertie (Pc), and emoji (So) all do NOT. So Python \w == \p{L} ∪ \p{N} ∪ {ASCII underscore} exactly — note \p{L} excludes _ (it is Pc), so _ must be listed literally, and other Pc chars must NOT be added.

FAILURE MODE with bare \w on "héllo 世界" (measured, Node): /\w+(?:\.?\w+)*/g yields ["h", "llo"] — 'é' is not a word char so the word is shredded at the accent — and "世界" produces ZERO matches, vanishing entirely. Then LowercaseFilter no-ops and StopFilter(minsize=2) drops "h", so the document indexes as the single meaningless term ["llo"]. The correct chain yields ["héllo", "世界"], both length>=2, both kept. Diagnostic framing: JS bare \w reproduces Python's re on BYTES, not str — I ran rb'\w+(\.?\w+)*' against the same input and got exactly [b'h', b'llo'] with the CJK gone. Porting with bare \w silently runs your tokenizer in bytes mode.

Why it is insidious rather than loud: (a) a CJK/Thai/Arabic document is inserted into the index but produces no terms, so it exists and matches nothing — zero recall, no exception; (b) the same broken analyzer runs on QUERIES, so searching "世界" produces an empty token list and an empty query that returns no hits rather than erroring, meaning index/query stay symmetrically wrong and ASCII-fixture round-trip tests keep passing; (c) the surviving fragments are worse than nothing — "llo" collides across unrelated accented words, so you get false positives alongside the false negatives; (d) accented ASCII-language text (French, Spanish, Vietnamese) degrades partially and plausibly, which reads as a relevance-tuning problem rather than a tokenizer bug. And critically: adding the u flag does NOT fix \w — unlike Python's re.UNICODE or PCRE's /u, JS \w stays [A-Za-z0-9_] under u and v. I verified /\w+/gu still splits 'héllo' into h/llo.
conclusions.confidence: High — measured in this session against both Python 3 re and Node, not recalled.
conclusions.implementation_note: Combining-marks decision, which you must make consciously: [\p{L}\p{N}_] is FAITHFUL to Python — I confirmed Python splits NFD 'héllo' into ['he','llo'] and so does this class. Adding \p{M} ([\p{L}\p{N}\p{M}_]) produces the BETTER answer ['héllo'] but diverges from Whoosh. Recommended: keep the faithful class and instead NFC-normalize with value.normalize('NFC') at both ingest and query time — that fixes decomposed input without changing behavior on composed input. Exception: if you must read or write an existing .whoosh index built by Python, do NOT normalize, because Whoosh has no normalization step and your terms would stop matching. Also mind that JS lacks re.finditer's guarantees around lastIndex — reuse of a /g regex across calls is stateful, so construct it per-call or reset lastIndex. \w+ cannot match empty so there is no zero-length-match infinite loop here, but preserve that property if you ever make the pattern more permissive.

risks: ITEM 3 IS THE ONE TO DISTRUST. The STOP_WORDS list is medium confidence and I may be off by a word or two. It is also the highest-blast-radius error because it fails silently and symmetrically (same wrong list on index and query), so tests pass while recall differs. Gate the port on running `python -c "from whoosh.analysis import STOP_WORDS; print(len(STOP_WORDS)); print(sorted(STOP_WORDS))"` and hardcoding the literal output. If len() != 34, my list is wrong.

Whoosh version drift: everything above reflects Whoosh 2.x as commonly documented. There is no Whoosh installed in /workspace, so I could not pin a version. If the source project uses whoosh-reloaded or a 3.x fork, default_pattern, STOP_WORDS, and the StandardAnalyzer chain are all plausible divergence points — check the actual installed package, not PyPI docs.

Silent-failure class in general: every default here (stoplist membership, minsize=2, the dot-bridging in the pattern, \w's Unicode scope) changes WHICH DOCUMENTS MATCH without ever raising. None of these produce a crash or a type error. Build a golden-corpus test (index N documents, assert the exact sorted term list per field) rather than relying on unit tests that round-trip through the port's own analyzer — a round-trip test cannot detect a symmetric analyzer bug.

Non-ASCII fixtures are mandatory in the test corpus. An ASCII-only test suite passes 100% with the bare-\w bug present. Include at minimum: CJK ('世界'), an accented Latin word in both NFC and NFD forms, an Arabic-Indic digit ('٣'), an astral-plane letter, an underscore identifier, a URL, and a decimal — those seven inputs discriminate every regex/normalization/length decision in item 7.

UTF-16 vs code-point counting leaks beyond the regex into minsize/maxsize (.length vs [...s].length) and into startChar/endChar offsets. JS offsets are self-consistent in UTF-16 units, but they are NOT comparable to Python character offsets for text containing astral characters. If highlighting or any stored offset crosses the Python/JS boundary, the spans will silently point at the wrong characters.

LowercaseFilter is not a trivial port either: Python str.lower() and JS toLowerCase() are both full Unicode case mappings but disagree on edge cases (e.g. U+0130 'İ', Cherokee, some length-changing mappings). This can make a term indexed by Python unfindable by the JS query analyzer even when the tokenizer is correct. Test the lowercase stage independently.

Not verified in this session and worth confirming from the real package: StopFilter's renumber=True default (affects phrase-query positions across removed stopwords), whether TEXT's phrase=True default is unchanged in your version, and the exact `_stored_<fieldname>` override behavior. I stated these with lower internal confidence than the numbered answers they sit inside.

Scope caveat: this covers only TEXT and ID as asked. KEYWORD (commas=False, lowercase=False, scorable=False), NGRAM/NGRAMWORDS, and NUMERIC each have their own defaults that will bite separately, and NUMERIC in particular does not use an analyzer at all.
